					<description><![CDATA[Wet fur forms a spiral of spiky hairs in this image by photographer Ben Dalgleish. For thin and flexible fibers like hair, a little moisture lets them clump together, forming stiffer (but still flexible) shapes. The technical term for this water-meets-flexible-solid phenomenon is elastocapillarity, and it lets you do things like wind a wire with [&#8230;]]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<p>Wet fur forms a spiral of spiky hairs in this image by photographer Ben Dalgleish. For thin and flexible fibers like hair, a little moisture lets them clump together, forming stiffer (but still flexible) shapes. The technical term for this water-meets-flexible-solid phenomenon is <a href="/tagged/elastocapillarity/">elastocapillarity</a>, and it lets you do things like <a href="/2017/01/its-often-at-the-intersection-of-topics-that-we/">wind a wire with a bubble</a>. It also makes a big difference when washing hair, including <a href="/2018/01/i-imagine-that-the-most-common-questions/">in space</a>. (Image credit: <a href="https://www.bwpawards.org/2026-winners">B. Dalgleish/BWPA</a>; via <a href="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/2026/03/british-wildlife-photography-awards-contest-winners/?__readwiseLocation=">Colossal</a>)</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img fetchpriority="high" decoding="async" width="1024" height="683" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/spiralling_texture_main-1024x683.png" alt="&quot;Spiralling Textures&quot; by Ben Dalgleish" class="wp-image-28974" srcset="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/spiralling_texture_main-1024x683.png 1024w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/spiralling_texture_main-300x200.png 300w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/spiralling_texture_main-768x512.png 768w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/spiralling_texture_main-1536x1025.png 1536w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/spiralling_texture_main-2048x1366.png 2048w" sizes="(max-width: 1024px) 100vw, 1024px" /></figure>
]]></content:encoded>

		<item>
		<title>Inside an Ear</title>
		<link>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/05/inside-an-ear/</link>
					<comments>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/05/inside-an-ear/#comments</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Nicole Sharp]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 07 May 2026 15:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Research]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[acoustics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[biology]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[cilia]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[fluid dynamics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[physics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[science]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[vibration]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://fyfluiddynamics.com/?p=29960</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[Our ears, like those of many other animals, convert mechanical signals to electrical ones, through a Rube-Goldberg-esque series of transformations. External sound waves make their way down the soft tube of the ear canal, which funnels them to a thin-walled cone, the eardrum, that&#8217;s about half as large as a dime. Here, the vibrating air [&#8230;]]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<p>Our ears, like those of many other animals, convert mechanical signals to electrical ones, through a Rube-Goldberg-esque series of transformations. External sound waves make their way down the soft tube of the ear canal, which funnels them to a thin-walled cone, the eardrum, that&#8217;s about half as large as a dime. Here, the vibrating air pushes against the cone’s membrane, and those <a href="/tagged/vibration/">vibrations</a> travel onward through a linked <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ossicles">trio of small bones</a> that amplify the vibration’s amplitude.</p>



<p>The last of these bones presses against an even smaller, oval-shaped membrane. As the bone moves, it shakes the membrane, sending waves through the liquid on its other side. Those waves travel down the spirals of the tiny, pea-sized <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochlea">cochlea</a>, named for a snail shell&#8217;s shape. As the waves move through the liquid, they bend <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hair_cell">bundles of hair-like strands</a> back and forth, like tall grass waving in a breeze. The bending triggers a chemical that binds to nerves at the base of the bundles, sending an electrical signal through the nerve and into the brain.</p>



<p>But the hair-like bundles, known as stereocilia, are also able to amplify incoming vibrations. In this case, the bundles in the outer portion of the cochlea expend energy to bend more than the incoming vibrations naturally make them move. This bending amplifies the fluid motion that gets transmitted to stereocilia further down the line; it&#8217;s those bundles that will make the final conversion to an electrical signal the brain receives. (Image credit: <a href="https://irp.nih.gov/our-research/research-in-action/high-fidelity-stereocilia">B. Kachar</a>; research credit: <a href="https://doi.org/10.1103/6wcm-z333">Y. Thipmaungprom et al.</a>; via <a href="https://physics.aps.org/articles/v19/45">APS</a>)</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image aligncenter size-full"><img decoding="async" width="1000" height="750" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/audtrans-Stereocilia.png" alt="Scanning electron microscope view of the stereocilia &quot;hair bundles&quot; inside a frog's inner ear." class="wp-image-29961" srcset="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/audtrans-Stereocilia.png 1000w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/audtrans-Stereocilia-300x225.png 300w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/audtrans-Stereocilia-768x576.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption class="wp-element-caption">Scanning electron microscope view of the stereocilia &#8220;hair bundles&#8221; inside a frog&#8217;s inner ear.</figcaption></figure>
]]></content:encoded>

		<title>Plucking Droplets</title>
		<link>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/05/plucking-droplets/</link>
					<comments>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/05/plucking-droplets/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Nicole Sharp]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Wed, 06 May 2026 15:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Phenomena]]></category>

					<description><![CDATA[A sudden breeze can pluck droplets hanging from a stem. Here, researchers recreate that phenomenon in the laboratory. With a close-up view and high-speed images, we can enjoy every detail of the detachment and break-up. As the wire pulls away, it drags a liquid sheet off the droplet. The thicker rims on either side of [&#8230;]]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<div class="wp-block-envira-envira-gallery"><div class="envira-gallery-feed-output"><img decoding="async" class="envira-gallery-feed-image" tabindex="0" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/pluck_drops1-1024x576.png" title="Wind shakes a plant stem, causing droplets to stretch and get plucked away. Text reads, &quot;A sudden blast of wind stretches the droplets and plucks them from the stem&quot;" alt="Wind shakes a plant stem, causing droplets to stretch and get plucked away. Text reads, &quot;A sudden blast of wind stretches the droplets and plucks them from the stem&quot;" /></div></div>



<p>A sudden breeze can <a href="/2025/06/droplet-on-a-plucked-wire/">pluck droplets</a> hanging from a stem. Here, researchers recreate that phenomenon in the laboratory. With a close-up view and high-speed images, we can enjoy every detail of the detachment and break-up. As the wire pulls away, it drags a liquid sheet off the droplet. The thicker rims on either side of the sheet eventually collide, creating a jet that stretches, deforms, and, at last, breaks. (Video and image credit: <a href="https://gfm.aps.org/meetings/dfd-2025/692e39eaa7f805227b16ff37">D. Maity et al.</a>)</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image aligncenter size-full"><img decoding="async" width="720" height="405" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/pluck_drops_main.gif" alt="Animation of two droplets getting plucked, one made of glycerin+water (left) and one of water (right)." class="wp-image-29989"/><figcaption class="wp-element-caption">Animation of two droplets getting plucked, one made of glycerin+water (left) and one of water (right).</figcaption></figure>

		<item>
		<title>Fluids Can Fracture</title>
		<link>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/05/fluids-can-fracture/</link>
					<comments>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/05/fluids-can-fracture/#comments</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Nicole Sharp]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Tue, 05 May 2026 15:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Research]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[fluid dynamics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[fracture]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[newtonian fluids]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[physics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[science]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[solid mechanics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[viscous flow]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://fyfluiddynamics.com/?p=29952</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[Fracture is a sudden, brittle breaking-apart that we generally associate with solid materials that get stressed too far. Some viscoelastic, non-Newtonian fluids have been known to fracture, but that was generally thought to be unusual. But a recent study turns that idea on its head, revealing that even simple, albeit highly viscous, liquids can fracture. [&#8230;]]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<p>Fracture is a sudden, brittle breaking-apart that we generally associate with solid materials that get stressed too far. Some <a href="/tagged/viscoelasticity">viscoelastic</a>, <a href="/tagged/non-Newtonian-fluids/">non-Newtonian fluids</a> have been known to fracture, but that was generally thought to be unusual. But a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1103/t2vy-32wr">recent study</a> turns that idea on its head, revealing that even simple, albeit highly viscous, liquids can fracture.</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image aligncenter size-full"><img loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="720" height="405" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/liquid_fracture1.gif" alt="A viscous hydrocarbon fluid gets stretched at 100 mm/s." class="wp-image-29955"/><figcaption class="wp-element-caption">A viscous hydrocarbon fluid gets stretched at 100 mm/s, drawing it into a thinning shape.</figcaption></figure>



<p>When you stretch a liquid, the general expectation is what you see above: the liquid gets drawn into an ever thinner shape. But researchers found that&#8211;when stretched quickly&#8211;that same simple hydrocarbon liquid cracked open:</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image aligncenter size-full"><img loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="720" height="405" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/liquid_fracture2.gif" alt="A viscous hydrocarbon fluid gets stretched at 300 mm/s, causing it to fracture like a solid." class="wp-image-29954"/><figcaption class="wp-element-caption">A viscous hydrocarbon fluid gets stretched at 300 mm/s, causing it to fracture like a solid.</figcaption></figure>



<p>There&#8217;s even an audible snap, which you can hear in the video below. The results were so surprising that they repeated the experiment several times and with different viscous (but Newtonian) liquids. The results held. When the liquids were pulled to a critical stress, they audibly snapped and fractured like a solid.</p>



<p>The next question, of course, is <em>why</em> this happens. The authors suspect (but have yet to show) that <a href="/tagged/cavitation">cavitation</a> may be at play in the initiation of the crack that separates the liquid in two. (Image, video, and research credit: <a href="https://doi.org/10.1103/t2vy-32wr">T. Lima et al.</a>; via <a href="https://gizmodo.com/liquids-crack-with-an-audible-snap-study-finds-2000740281?__readwiseLocation=">Gizmodo</a>)</p>



<figure class="wp-block-embed is-type-video is-provider-youtube wp-block-embed-youtube wp-embed-aspect-16-9 wp-has-aspect-ratio"><div class="wp-block-embed__wrapper">
<iframe loading="lazy" title="Scientists Discover Unexpected Fracturing Behavior in Liquids" width="500" height="281" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/i5TQegTyCvc?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>
</div></figure>
]]></content:encoded>

		<title>Meandering Along the Alabama River</title>
		<link>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/05/meandering-along-the-alabama-river/</link>
					<comments>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/05/meandering-along-the-alabama-river/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Nicole Sharp]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Mon, 04 May 2026 15:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Phenomena]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[astronaut]]></category>

		<category><![CDATA[science]]></category>

					<description><![CDATA[Over time, rivers naturally curve and meander. As water accelerates around a river bend&#8217;s curve, it creates a secondary flow that carves sediment away from the outer bank and deposits it on the inner one. That, in turn, makes the river bend sharper until it eventually cuts part of the river off into an oxbow [&#8230;]]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<p>Over time, rivers naturally curve and meander. As water accelerates around a river bend&#8217;s curve, it creates <a href="/2014/05/when-unconstrained-by-the-local-topography-rivers/">a secondary flow</a> that carves sediment away from the outer bank and deposits it on the inner one. That, in turn, makes the river bend sharper until it eventually cuts part of the river off into an <a href="/tagged/oxbow-lake/">oxbow lake</a>. In this <a href="/tagged/astronaut/">astronaut</a> photo, we see the Alabama River flowing right-to-left. The river&#8217;s natural meander is constrained by the dam on the center left, which widens the river upstream. The higher water level upstream creates the feather-like floodplains lining the river.  (Image credit: NASA; via <a href="https://earthobservatory.nasa.gov/images/153384/bends-of-the-alabama-river">NASA Earth Observatory</a>)</p>
]]></content:encoded>

But despite first appearances, each photograph is true to life; the fabrics are suspended on taut lines. Their dance is driven by wind energy, drag, tension, and flow&#8211;not manipulated pixels. 										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<div class="wp-block-envira-envira-gallery"><div class="envira-gallery-feed-output"><img decoding="async" class="envira-gallery-feed-image" tabindex="0" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/jackson3-1024x769.png" title="Image by Thomas Jackson." alt="Image by Thomas Jackson." /></div></div>



<p>Fabrics flutter in seemingly impossible ways in artist <a href="https://thomasjacksonphotography.com/">Thomas Jackson</a>&#8216;s images. But despite first appearances, each photograph is true to life; the fabrics are suspended on taut lines. Their <a href="/2012/08/the-flapping-of-flexible-objects-like-flags-have/">dance</a> is driven by wind energy, drag, tension, and flow&#8211;not manipulated pixels. I love the (turbulent) energy of them! (Image credit: <a href="https://thomasjacksonphotography.com/">T. Jackson</a>; via <a href="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/2026/03/thomas-jackson-fabrics-landscapes-photographs/?__readwiseLocation=">Colossal</a>)</p>

		<item>
		<title>Recreating Atmospheres</title>
		<link>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/04/recreating-atmospheres/</link>
					<comments>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/04/recreating-atmospheres/#comments</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Nicole Sharp]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 30 Apr 2026 15:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Research]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[atmospheric science]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[energy cascade]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[flow visualization]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[fluid dynamics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[physics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[planetary science]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[rotating flow]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[science]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[turbulence]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[vorticity]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://fyfluiddynamics.com/?p=29751</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[In planetary atmospheres, energy and vorticity can cascade from large scales to smaller ones, but the mechanics of this transfer remain somewhat elusive. In a recent experiment, researchers built a lab-scale representation of an atmosphere using a meter-scale rotating annular tank. The outer bottom edge of the tank gets heated&#8211;representing the sun&#8217;s warming at the [&#8230;]]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<p>In planetary atmospheres, energy and <a href="/tagged/vorticity/">vorticity</a> can cascade from large scales to smaller ones, but the mechanics of this transfer remain somewhat elusive. In a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1103/n2nj-dg5r">recent experiment</a>, researchers built a lab-scale representation of an atmosphere using a meter-scale rotating annular tank. The outer bottom edge of the tank gets heated&#8211;representing the sun&#8217;s warming at the equator&#8211;while a pipe in the center of the tank gets cooled near the tank surface, which mimics the chilling effect of the poles. Researchers filled the tank with a water-glycerol mixture and recorded how their artificial atmosphere responded at different rotation rates.</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image aligncenter size-full"><img loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="720" height="360" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/geo_model_ani.gif" alt="Two different rotating atmospheres, colored by vorticity (red clockwise, blue counterclockwise). The left version has a slower rate of rotation, and thus larger length scales." class="wp-image-29754"/><figcaption class="wp-element-caption">Two different rotating atmospheres, colored by vorticity (red clockwise, blue counterclockwise). The left version has a slower rate of rotation, and thus larger length scales.</figcaption></figure>



<p>The results show an energy spectrum that&#8217;s consistent with atmospheric observations&#8211;with a steep drop at large length scales and a flatter one at smaller scales. But interestingly, they also found that the cascade was temperature-dependent in ways that current models don&#8217;t predict. Untangling that effect could help us understand not only our atmosphere but those of other planets. (Image credit: tank &#8211; H. Scolan, animation &#8211; <a href="https://doi.org/10.1103/n2nj-dg5r">S. Ding et al.</a>; research credit: <a href="https://doi.org/10.1103/n2nj-dg5r">S. Ding et al.</a>; via <a href="https://physics.aps.org/articles/v19/40?__readwiseLocation=">APS</a>)</p>
]]></content:encoded>

		<item>
		<title>Bouncing on a Wave</title>
		<link>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/04/bouncing-on-a-wave/</link>
					<comments>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/04/bouncing-on-a-wave/#comments</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Nicole Sharp]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Wed, 29 Apr 2026 15:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Phenomena]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[2025gofm]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[bouncing droplets]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[coalescence]]></category>

<div class="wp-block-envira-envira-gallery"><div class="envira-gallery-feed-output"><img decoding="async" class="envira-gallery-feed-image" tabindex="0" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/wave_waltz1-1024x576.png" title="Droplets bouncing on a vibrating fluid surface. Text reads, &quot;This is a collection of walking droplets bouncing on the surface of a vertically vibrated fluid interface...&quot;" alt="Droplets bouncing on a vibrating fluid surface. Text reads, &quot;This is a collection of walking droplets bouncing on the surface of a vertically vibrated fluid interface...&quot;" /></div></div>



<p> On a <a href="/tagged/vibration">vibrating</a> fluid, <a href="/tagged/bouncing-droplets/">droplets can bounce</a> and interact in complex ways. Here, researchers demonstrate some of the peculiar dynamics of these wave-guided droplets, showing how they can do things like pair up in waltzes. To keep the droplets from <a href="/tagged/coalescence/">coalescing</a> with one another, they perform their experiments in a pressurized chamber; the higher air pressure makes it harder for the air film between droplets to drain during a collision, making the droplets unable to coalesce. Under these conditions, the authors show that the droplet-wave system has <a href="/tagged/hydrodynamic-quantum-analogs/">quantum-like statistics</a>. (Video and image credit: J. Clampett et al.)</p>
]]></content:encoded>

		<title>&#8220;Sidewall Symphony&#8221;</title>
		<link>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/04/sidewall-symphony/</link>
					<comments>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/04/sidewall-symphony/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Nicole Sharp]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Tue, 28 Apr 2026 15:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Research]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[2025gofm]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[flow visualization]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[fluid dynamics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[fluids as art]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[physics]]></category>

		<category><![CDATA[turbulence]]></category>

					<description><![CDATA[Flow visualization is both an art and science in fluid dynamics. Here, researchers were interested in studying the separation bubble that forms over a backward-facing ramp&#8211;a shape that shows up, for example, on an aircraft. In these areas, the flow over the surface separates, leaving an unsteady, recirculating bubble. That&#8217;s the flow that researchers are [&#8230;]]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<p><a href="/tagged/flow-visualization/">Flow visualization</a> is both an art and science in fluid dynamics. Here, researchers were interested in studying the <a href="/tagged/flow-separation/">separation bubble</a> that forms over a backward-facing ramp&#8211;a shape that shows up, for example, on an aircraft. In these areas, the flow over the surface separates, leaving an unsteady, recirculating bubble. </p>



<p>That&#8217;s the flow that researchers are visualizing here. They&#8217;ve done so by adding tiny helium-filled soap bubbles to the flow. With bright lights illuminating the bubbles, each one leaves a streak in a photograph, showing where the bubble moved during the time the camera&#8217;s shutter was open. Although images like these are beautiful, they can also be analyzed by computers to extract  the underlying flow that created the image. (Image and research credit: <a href="https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-fluid-mechanics/article/threedimensional-lowfrequency-dynamics-of-a-turbulent-separation-bubble/4ABB5AA0338669640C5374D52E0BA58E#article">B. Steinfurth et al.</a>; see also <a href="https://gfm.aps.org/meetings/dfd-2025/692e39e3a7f805227b16fe68">here</a>)</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image aligncenter size-large"><img loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1024" height="723" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/sidewall_symphony_main-1024x723.png" alt="A research poster showing streaks left by hydrogen bubbles in the flow over a backward-facing ramp." class="wp-image-28633" srcset="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/sidewall_symphony_main-1024x723.png 1024w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/sidewall_symphony_main-300x212.png 300w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/sidewall_symphony_main-768x542.png 768w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/sidewall_symphony_main-1536x1085.png 1536w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/sidewall_symphony_main.png 1600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1024px) 100vw, 1024px" /></figure>
]]></content:encoded>

		<title>A Colorful Glimpse</title>
		<link>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/04/a-colorful-glimpse/</link>
					<comments>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/04/a-colorful-glimpse/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Nicole Sharp]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Mon, 27 Apr 2026 15:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Phenomena]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[flow visualization]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[fluid dynamics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[physics]]></category>

					<description><![CDATA[Peeking between the clouds, satellites caught a glimpse of a massive phytoplankton bloom off the coast of Greenland in May 2024. The tiny organisms may be visible only under a microscope, but gatherings like these stretch hundreds of kilometers and are visible from space. Like tracer particles in a flow, the phytoplankton outline the swirls [&#8230;]]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<p>Peeking between the clouds, satellites caught a glimpse of a massive <a href="/tagged/phytoplankton/">phytoplankton</a> bloom off the coast of Greenland in May 2024. The tiny organisms may be visible only under a microscope, but gatherings like these stretch hundreds of kilometers and are visible from space. Like <a href="/tagged/flow-visualization/">tracer particles in a flow</a>, the phytoplankton outline the swirls and eddies of the underlying ocean. (Image credit: L. Dauphin; via <a href="https://earthobservatory.nasa.gov/images/152953/peek-a-bloom-in-the-north-atlantic">NASA Earth Observatory</a>)</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1024" height="682" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/greenlandbloom_amo_20240616_lrg_main-1024x682.png" alt="A satellite image reveals the blue and green swirls of a phytoplankton bloom." class="wp-image-21903" srcset="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/greenlandbloom_amo_20240616_lrg_main-1024x682.png 1024w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/greenlandbloom_amo_20240616_lrg_main-300x200.png 300w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/greenlandbloom_amo_20240616_lrg_main-768x512.png 768w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/greenlandbloom_amo_20240616_lrg_main-1536x1024.png 1536w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/greenlandbloom_amo_20240616_lrg_main-270x180.png 270w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/greenlandbloom_amo_20240616_lrg_main-710x473.png 710w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/greenlandbloom_amo_20240616_lrg_main.png 2000w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1024px) 100vw, 1024px" /><figcaption class="wp-element-caption">A satellite image reveals the blue and green swirls of a phytoplankton bloom.</figcaption></figure>
]]></content:encoded>
